title: Node.js
description: How Node.js really works: V8 and libuv, the event loop, modules and npm, streams, errors, concurrency, performance and the modern built-in toolchain. Built for backend interview prep.

chapters.title: The Node.js runtime: V8, libuv and non-blocking I/O
chapters.summary: What Node.js is made of, why a single JavaScript thread can serve thousands of connections, and how releases work.

lesson.heading: What Node.js actually is
lesson.body:
Node.js is a JavaScript runtime: a C++ program that embeds Google's **V8** engine to execute JavaScript and adds the APIs a server needs (files, sockets, processes, timers, crypto). The browser gives JavaScript the DOM; Node gives it the operating system.

The main building blocks:

- **V8** compiles JavaScript to machine code (Ignition interpreter, then optimizing tiers such as Maglev and TurboFan) and manages the heap and garbage collection.
- **libuv** is a C library that provides the event loop, async networking, timers and a thread pool for work the OS cannot do asynchronously.
- **Bindings and core modules** (`node:fs`, `node:http`, `node:crypto`...) are JavaScript wrappers over C++ bindings that call libuv, OpenSSL, zlib, llhttp, simdjson and friends.

When you run `node app.js`, Node boots V8, loads your module, runs its top-level code to completion, then enters the event loop and keeps running as long as there is pending work (open servers, timers, in-flight requests).

lesson.heading: Single-threaded JavaScript, multi-threaded runtime
lesson.body:
Your JavaScript runs on **one main thread**. Only one callback executes at a time, so you never need locks around plain JS objects. But Node as a process is not single-threaded: V8 uses helper threads for GC and compilation, and libuv owns a **thread pool** (default 4 threads, set with `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, max 1024).

Network I/O does not use the thread pool. libuv hands sockets to the kernel's readiness APIs (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows) and gets notified when data arrives. The thread pool is used for things without good async OS APIs: most `fs` operations, `dns.lookup`, and CPU-heavy `crypto` and `zlib` calls like `crypto.pbkdf2` or `zlib.gzip`.

This is why a Node server can hold 10,000 idle WebSocket connections cheaply: each connection is a file descriptor watched by the kernel, not a thread with its own stack.

lesson.heading: Non-blocking I/O and why blocking the loop hurts
lesson.body:
Node's model is: start an operation, register a callback (or await a promise), and return to the event loop immediately. When the OS reports completion, the callback is queued and runs when the stack is empty.

The flip side: anything that keeps the main thread busy blocks **every** request. A 200 ms synchronous JSON parse of a huge payload, a catastrophic regex, `fs.readFileSync` in a request handler or a tight loop all freeze the whole server for that time.

Rules of thumb:

- Use async APIs in request paths; sync APIs (`readFileSync`) are fine at startup.
- Move CPU-heavy work to `worker_threads`, a separate service, or a job queue.
- Split big loops into chunks or stream data instead of buffering it all.

lesson.heading: Globals and the process object
lesson.body:
Node has `globalThis` (aliased as `global`) plus web-standard globals: `fetch`, `URL`, `AbortController`, `TextEncoder`, `structuredClone`, `setTimeout`, `queueMicrotask`, `crypto` (Web Crypto), `WebSocket` (client, stable since Node 22) and `Blob`.

`process` describes the running process: `process.argv` (command-line args), `process.env` (environment variables, always strings), `process.exitCode`, `process.memoryUsage()`, `process.pid`, `process.platform`, and events like `exit`, `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`.

Prefer setting `process.exitCode = 1` and letting the process finish naturally over calling `process.exit(1)`, which terminates immediately and can cut off pending writes such as logs flushing to stdout.

lesson.heading: Release lines and LTS
lesson.body:
Node ships a new major every six months (April and October). **Even-numbered** majors enter **Long Term Support** in October and receive fixes for about 30 months total; odd-numbered majors are short-lived Current releases. Production systems should run an Active or Maintenance LTS line.

As of late 2026 the supported LTS lines are Node 22 (maintenance) and Node 24, with Node 26 entering LTS in October 2026. Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026. Check the official release schedule before choosing a version, and pin it with `.nvmrc`, the `engines` field, or your container base image.

Version managers like nvm, fnm or Volta let you switch versions per project. Corepack (bundled with Node up to v24, then distributed separately) manages pnpm and Yarn versions declared in the `packageManager` field.

keyPoints: Node.js = V8 (executes JS) + libuv (event loop, async I/O, thread pool) + C++ bindings and core modules.
Your JavaScript runs on one main thread; the runtime itself uses several threads.
Network I/O uses OS readiness APIs (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), not the libuv thread pool.
The thread pool (default 4) serves most fs work, dns.lookup, and heavy crypto and zlib calls.
Blocking the main thread stalls every connection; keep request paths async and offload CPU work.
Prefer process.exitCode over process.exit() so pending I/O can flush.
Even-numbered majors become LTS; run an LTS line in production.

questions.prompt: Which component provides Node's event loop and thread pool?
questions.explanation: libuv is the C library that implements the event loop, cross-platform async I/O and the worker thread pool. V8 only executes JavaScript and manages its heap.

questions.prompt: What is the default size of the libuv thread pool?
questions.explanation: The default is 4 threads. You can change it with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable (up to 1024), which must be set before the pool is first used.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations does NOT use the libuv thread pool?
options: A TCP socket read on an http server
questions.explanation: Socket I/O is handled by the kernel's readiness mechanism (epoll/kqueue/IOCP). File system calls, pbkdf2 and zlib compression run on the thread pool because they block or are CPU-heavy.

questions.prompt: A request handler calls a function that runs a 300 ms synchronous loop. What happens to other requests during that time?
options: They are handled by other threads in parallel
They wait; nothing else runs on the main thread until the loop finishes
Node automatically moves the loop to a worker
They fail with a timeout error immediately
questions.explanation: All JavaScript callbacks share one main thread. A synchronous loop holds it, so every other request waits in the queue until it finishes. Node never moves JS to another thread automatically.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Top-level code runs to completion first. The timer callback can only run after the call stack is empty and the event loop reaches the timers phase, even with a 0 ms delay.

questions.prompt: Which release line should a new production service target?
options: An Active or Maintenance LTS (even-numbered) release
Any release, they are all supported for 3 years
questions.explanation: Even-numbered majors enter LTS and get roughly 30 months of fixes. Odd-numbered releases are only supported for a short time and are meant for trying new features.

questions.prompt: Because JavaScript in Node runs on a single thread, a Node process never uses more than one OS thread.
questions.explanation: Only your JS callbacks run on the main thread. libuv's thread pool, V8's GC and compiler threads, and any worker_threads you create are additional OS threads.

questions.prompt: Values in process.env are always strings (or undefined).
questions.explanation: Environment variables are strings at the OS level. Setting process.env.PORT = 3000 stores "3000", so parse numbers and booleans explicitly.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are available as globals in modern Node without importing anything?
questions.explanation: fetch, AbortController and structuredClone are web-standard globals in Node. document is browser-only. Node's localStorage implementation is experimental and needs a flag and storage file, so it is not a default global you can rely on.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the environment variable ___ changes the number of libuv thread pool threads.
questions.explanation: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE sets the pool size. It must be set before the pool is first used, ideally in the environment that launches node.

questions.prompt: Explain how Node.js can handle thousands of concurrent connections with a single JavaScript thread.
questions.answer:
- Node uses an event-driven, non-blocking model: I/O is started and the thread immediately goes back to the event loop instead of waiting.
- For sockets, libuv registers file descriptors with the kernel (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) and is notified when they are readable or writable, so idle connections cost almost nothing (no thread per connection, no stack per connection).
- When an operation completes, its callback is queued and run on the main thread; each callback should be short.
- Operations without good async OS support (file system, dns.lookup, some crypto/zlib) run on libuv's thread pool and report back to the loop.
- The trade-off: CPU-bound work blocks everything, so it must be chunked, moved to worker_threads, or offloaded to another service.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between V8 and Node.js?
questions.answer:
V8 is Google's JavaScript and WebAssembly engine: it parses, compiles (Ignition, Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan) and executes JS, and manages the heap and garbage collector. It knows nothing about files, sockets or timers.
Node.js is a runtime that embeds V8 and adds the host environment: libuv for the event loop and async I/O, core modules like fs, http, net and crypto, the module loaders (CommonJS and ESM), npm integration and process-level APIs.
Chrome also embeds V8 but provides browser APIs (DOM, fetch, Web Workers) instead. Other runtimes make different choices: Deno embeds V8 with a Rust host, Bun uses JavaScriptCore.

questions.prompt: When would you NOT choose Node.js for a backend service?
questions.answer:
- Heavy CPU-bound workloads (video encoding, large numeric computation, ML inference) where you would spend most of the time fighting the single main thread; Go, Rust, Java or Python with native libraries may fit better, or Node can orchestrate while workers do the compute.
- When the team and ecosystem are strongly elsewhere (e.g. existing JVM platform with shared libraries).
- Node shines for I/O-bound APIs, BFFs, realtime (WebSockets), streaming and tooling, and when sharing TypeScript types between frontend and backend is valuable.
A good answer acknowledges that worker_threads exist but adds complexity, and that many CPU-heavy tasks can be pushed to queues or specialised services.

questions.prompt: Why is calling process.exit() inside a request handler or after logging often a bug?
questions.answer:
process.exit() terminates synchronously: pending asynchronous work is abandoned. Writes to stdout/stderr are asynchronous for pipes on POSIX, so log lines can be lost, open DB transactions are not committed, and in-flight HTTP responses are cut off.
Better options: set process.exitCode and let the event loop drain; for shutdown, stop accepting connections (server.close()), finish in-flight work with a timeout, close pools, then exit. Reserve process.exit() for truly unrecoverable states, ideally after a hard timeout.

chapters.title: Modules: CommonJS vs ES Modules
chapters.summary: How require and import differ, how Node decides which loader to use, and how to interoperate between the two systems.

lesson.heading: Two module systems
lesson.body:
Node supports **CommonJS** (CJS, the original system: `require` and `module.exports`) and **ECMAScript Modules** (ESM, the language standard: `import` and `export`). New code should prefer ESM, but you will meet CJS in older packages and codebases for years.

Key differences:

- **Loading**: `require` is synchronous and runs the file immediately. ESM is parsed first, its static import graph is linked, then modules are evaluated, which allows top-level `await`.
- **Bindings**: CJS exports a value copy (an object you get back). ESM exports are **live bindings**: if the exporting module reassigns an exported `let`, importers see the new value.
- **Strictness**: ESM is always strict mode; `this` at the top level is `undefined` (in CJS it is `module.exports`).
- **Paths**: ESM imports of relative files need the full file extension (`./util.js`); `require` resolves `./util` by trying extensions.

lesson.heading: How Node chooses CJS or ESM
lesson.body:
Node decides per file:

- `.mjs` is always ESM, `.cjs` is always CommonJS.
- `.js` follows the nearest `package.json` `"type"` field: `"module"` means ESM, `"commonjs"` or missing means CJS.
- Since Node 22.7 / 20.19, **syntax detection** is on by default: a `.js` file with no `type` that contains ESM syntax is run as ESM. Being explicit with `"type"` is still best practice and avoids a double parse.

Use the `node:` prefix for built-ins (`import fs from "node:fs"`). It is unambiguous, cannot be shadowed by an npm package, and is required for some newer modules such as `node:test` and `node:sqlite`.

lesson.heading: Missing CJS globals in ESM
lesson.body:
ESM files do not have `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` or `__dirname`. Use `import.meta` instead:

- `import.meta.url` is the file URL of the current module.
- `import.meta.filename` and `import.meta.dirname` (Node 20.11+) give absolute paths.
- `createRequire(import.meta.url)` from `node:module` gives you a `require` function when you really need one.
- JSON can be imported with an import attribute: `import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }`.

lesson.heading: Interop: importing CJS and requiring ESM
lesson.body:
**ESM importing CJS** always works: `module.exports` becomes the default export, and Node statically detects many named exports so `import { readFileSync } from "some-cjs"` usually works too.

**CJS requiring ESM** used to be impossible (you had to use dynamic `import()`, which returns a promise). Since Node 22.12 and 20.19, `require(esm)` is enabled by default, as long as the ES module graph has **no top-level await**. If it does, `require` throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` and you must use `import()`.

Dynamic `import()` works in both systems and is also how you lazy-load a module only when needed.

lesson.heading: Package entry points and the exports field
lesson.body:
The `exports` field in `package.json` defines a package's public entry points and blocks deep imports of anything not listed. Conditional exports let one package serve different files to `import` and `require` callers.

Beware the **dual package hazard**: if a package ships separate CJS and ESM builds, an app can end up loading both copies, giving you two instances of the same class or singleton state. Mitigations: ship ESM only (now practical thanks to `require(esm)`), or make one build a thin wrapper around the other.

lesson.heading: Module caching and circular dependencies
lesson.body:
Both systems cache modules: a module's top-level code runs once, and later imports get the same instance. That is why a module-level `const pool = new Pool()` acts like a singleton.

In CJS, `require.cache` is keyed by resolved filename. In a circular `require`, the second module receives the first module's **partially populated** `module.exports`, which commonly shows up as `undefined` functions. In ESM, circular imports work with live bindings, but accessing a binding before its module has evaluated throws a `ReferenceError` (temporal dead zone). The real fix is usually to extract shared code into a third module.

keyPoints: Prefer ESM (import/export) for new code; CJS (require/module.exports) remains common in older packages.
.mjs is always ESM, .cjs is always CJS, .js follows package.json "type".
ESM exports are live bindings; CJS gives you whatever object module.exports held.
In ESM use import.meta.dirname/filename/url instead of __dirname and __filename.
require(esm) works by default in Node 22.12+ and 20.19+ unless the ESM graph uses top-level await.
The exports field defines public entry points and conditional import/require targets.
Modules are cached; circular dependencies can expose partially initialised exports.

questions.prompt: A project has no "type" field in package.json. How is a file named server.cjs treated?
questions.explanation: The .cjs extension always means CommonJS regardless of package.json. Likewise .mjs is always ESM. Only .js files depend on the "type" field (and syntax detection).

questions.prompt: Which line correctly gets the current directory inside an ES module on modern Node?
questions.explanation: __dirname is not defined in ESM. import.meta.dirname (Node 20.11+) gives the module's directory. process.cwd() is the working directory of the process, which can differ from the file's location.

questions.prompt: What does this ESM program print?
options: It throws because count is constant
questions.explanation: ESM exports are live bindings. main.mjs sees the current value of count, so after increment() runs it reads 1. A CommonJS module exporting a primitive would give a copy instead.

questions.prompt: In a CommonJS file on Node 24, you call require("./esm-lib.mjs") and the module uses top-level await. What happens?
options: It works and returns a promise
It silently returns an empty object
It blocks until the await resolves
questions.explanation: require(esm) is synchronous, so it only supports ES module graphs without top-level await. Otherwise Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE and you must use dynamic import().

questions.prompt: An ESM file contains import { helper } from "./helper"; and helper.js exists. What happens?
options: ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND because ESM requires the extension
It works only with a bundler flag
questions.explanation: Node's ESM resolver does not guess extensions or directory indexes for relative imports. You must write "./helper.js". TypeScript projects using NodeNext resolution enforce the same rule.

questions.prompt: What does the "exports" field in package.json do?
options: Defines the package's public entry points and blocks unlisted deep imports
Marks which functions are exported from index.js
questions.explanation: exports maps subpaths (".", "./utils") to files, supports conditions like import, require and types, and makes any unlisted path inaccessible to consumers (ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED).

questions.prompt: A module's top-level code runs every time it is imported or required.
questions.explanation: Modules are cached after the first load. Subsequent imports return the same instance, which is why module-level state behaves like a singleton within one process.

questions.prompt: Dynamic import() can be used from both CommonJS and ES modules.
questions.explanation: import() is available in both systems and returns a promise of the module namespace. It is the standard way to load ESM from CJS when require(esm) is not possible, and to lazy-load code.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are NOT available by default inside an ES module?
questions.explanation: __filename, require and module.exports are CommonJS wrapper variables. ESM provides import.meta.url and supports top-level await. createRequire can recreate require if needed.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: to load JSON in ESM you write import data from "./data.json" ___ { type: "json" };
questions.explanation: Import attributes use the with keyword. The older assert keyword was removed from V8 and Node in favour of with.

questions.prompt: Compare CommonJS and ES Modules. Which would you use for a new Node.js project and why?
questions.answer:
- CJS: require is synchronous and dynamic (can be called anywhere, with computed paths), exports a plain object, wraps files in a function providing __dirname, require, module.
- ESM: static import/export syntax, parsed and linked before execution, live bindings, strict mode, top-level await, standard across browsers and runtimes, and enables tree shaking in bundlers.
- For new projects I'd use ESM ("type": "module"), node: prefixed built-ins, and explicit file extensions. Since require(esm) is available in current LTS lines, shipping ESM-only libraries no longer strands CJS consumers unless top-level await is used.
- I'd keep CJS only where tooling still requires it, and be aware of the dual package hazard if publishing both builds.

questions.prompt: What is the dual package hazard and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer:
When a package ships both a CJS and an ESM build, one app can load both: one dependency requires it, another imports it. You get two copies of module state, so singletons, caches, instanceof checks and registered plugins diverge silently.
Avoid it by: publishing ESM only (viable now that require(esm) is default); or making the ESM entry a thin wrapper that re-exports the CJS build (or vice versa) so there is one real instance; or keeping state out of the module (pass instances explicitly).

questions.prompt: A teammate reports that a function imported from another module is undefined at runtime, but only in some code paths. How would you investigate?
questions.answer:
My first suspect is a circular dependency. In CJS, if a.js requires b.js and b.js requires a.js, b receives a's module.exports before a has finished assigning it, so the destructured functions are undefined. In ESM it would surface as a ReferenceError for accessing a binding before initialization.
Steps: check the import chain (tools like madge can draw the graph), log at module top level to see the evaluation order, and look for index.js barrel files that re-export everything, which often create hidden cycles.
Fix by moving the shared code into a separate module both can import, deferring the require into the function that needs it, or using dependency injection instead of module-level imports.

chapters.title: npm, package.json, semver and lockfiles
chapters.summary: Manage dependencies predictably: semver ranges, lockfiles, npm ci, scripts and supply-chain hygiene.

lesson.heading: package.json essentials
lesson.body:
`package.json` describes your project: its name and version, the module type, scripts, the Node version it supports, and its dependencies.

- `dependencies`: needed at runtime.
- `devDependencies`: only for building and testing (TypeScript, test runners, linters). Skipped with `npm ci --omit=dev`.
- `peerDependencies`: a library declares the host package it plugs into (a React component library peers on `react`). npm 7+ installs peers automatically and errors on conflicts.
- `optionalDependencies`: install failures are tolerated.
- `engines`: the supported Node versions. npm only warns unless `engine-strict` is set.

lesson.heading: Semantic versioning and ranges
lesson.body:
Semver versions are `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes.

Common range operators:

- `^1.4.2` (caret, npm's default): `>=1.4.2 <2.0.0`. Allows minor and patch updates.
- `~1.4.2` (tilde): `>=1.4.2 <1.5.0`. Patch updates only.
- `1.4.2`: exactly that version.
- `*` or `latest`: anything (avoid).

Gotcha: for `0.x` versions the caret is stricter because 0.x is treated as unstable. `^0.4.2` means `>=0.4.2 <0.5.0`, and `^0.0.3` means exactly `0.0.3`.

Pre-release versions like `2.0.0-beta.1` are only matched by a range that explicitly includes a pre-release on the same `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.

lesson.heading: Lockfiles, npm install and npm ci
lesson.body:
Ranges are resolved at install time, so two installs a week apart can produce different trees. The lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `bun.lock`) records the exact resolved version, tarball URL and integrity hash of every package in the tree. **Commit it** for applications.

- `npm install` resolves ranges, may update the lockfile, and installs.
- `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` and installs **exactly** what the lockfile says. It fails if `package.json` and the lockfile disagree. Use it in CI and Docker builds for reproducible, faster installs.
- `npm update` moves packages to the newest version allowed by their ranges and updates the lockfile.
- `npm outdated` shows what is behind.

Libraries publish without a lockfile effect: consumers resolve the library's ranges against their own tree. That is why library authors should test against the range they declare.

lesson.heading: Scripts, npx and workspaces
lesson.body:
`npm run <name>` runs a script with `node_modules/.bin` on the PATH, so locally installed CLIs work without global installs. `pre` and `post` hooks (`pretest`, `posttest`) run automatically. `npm test` and `npm start` are shortcuts.

`npx <pkg>` runs a package binary, downloading it temporarily if not installed. Node 22 also has `node --run <script>`, a faster built-in way to run package.json scripts (it skips pre/post hooks).

**Workspaces** (`"workspaces": ["packages/*"]`) manage a monorepo with one lockfile and links between local packages. pnpm is popular here because its content-addressable store and strict, symlinked `node_modules` prevent using undeclared (phantom) dependencies.

lesson.heading: Supply-chain security
lesson.body:
Every dependency is code that runs with your app's permissions, and install scripts (`preinstall`, `postinstall`) run arbitrary code at install time. Real incidents include typosquatting, hijacked maintainer accounts publishing malicious versions, and self-propagating worms (the 2025 Shai-Hulud attack stole npm tokens and republished infected packages).

Practical defenses:

- Commit lockfiles and use `npm ci` so new versions arrive only through reviewed PRs.
- Run `npm audit` (or Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk) and fix critical advisories.
- Disable install scripts where possible (`npm ci --ignore-scripts`, pnpm blocks dependency build scripts by default since v10).
- Use a release-age delay for new versions (pnpm `minimumReleaseAge`, Renovate `minimumReleaseAge`).
- Prefer packages with provenance attestations, and use trusted publishing (OIDC from CI) instead of long-lived npm tokens for your own packages.
- Use `overrides` in package.json to force a patched version of a transitive dependency.

keyPoints: dependencies are runtime needs; devDependencies are build/test tools; peerDependencies declare the host a plugin needs.
^1.2.3 allows <2.0.0, ~1.2.3 allows <1.3.0; for 0.x the caret only allows patch-level changes within the same minor.
Commit the lockfile for applications; it pins exact versions and integrity hashes.
Use npm ci in CI and Docker: clean, exact, fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree.
npm run puts node_modules/.bin on the PATH; node --run is a faster built-in runner.
Install scripts and compromised packages are real attack vectors; audit, pin and limit scripts.
overrides force a version of a transitive dependency.

questions.prompt: Which versions satisfy the range ^2.3.1?
questions.explanation: The caret allows changes that do not modify the left-most non-zero digit. For 2.3.1 that is the major, so minor and patch updates are allowed up to <3.0.0.

questions.prompt: Which versions satisfy ^0.4.2?
questions.explanation: For 0.x versions the minor is the left-most non-zero digit, so the caret locks it: >=0.4.2 <0.5.0. Pre-1.0 versions are treated as unstable, where a minor bump can break things.

questions.prompt: What does npm ci do differently from npm install?
options: It removes node_modules and installs exactly what the lockfile specifies, failing on mismatch
It updates all packages to latest
questions.explanation: npm ci is for automated environments: it never writes to package.json or the lockfile, starts from a clean node_modules, and errors out if the lockfile is out of sync with package.json.

questions.prompt: A security fix is in a transitive dependency's patch release, but your direct dependency pins an old range. What is the quickest correct fix in npm?
options: Add an overrides entry in package.json forcing the patched version
questions.explanation: overrides tells npm to replace a version anywhere in the tree. Hand edits to node_modules are lost on the next install, and deleting the lockfile changes many other versions unpredictably.

questions.prompt: Which semver bump is right when you remove a public function from your library?
questions.explanation: Removing or changing public API breaks consumers, which requires a MAJOR bump. Added backward-compatible features are MINOR; bug fixes are PATCH.

questions.prompt: Your package is a React component library. How should it declare react?
questions.explanation: A peer dependency means the host app provides react, so only one copy exists at runtime. Putting it in dependencies risks two Reacts, which breaks hooks. It is also listed in devDependencies so the library's own tests can run.

questions.prompt: Applications should commit package-lock.json to version control.
questions.explanation: The lockfile is what makes installs reproducible across machines, CI and production. Without it each install can resolve different versions.

questions.prompt: npm only runs a package's postinstall script if you explicitly approve it.
questions.explanation: npm runs lifecycle scripts of dependencies by default during install, which is why malicious postinstall scripts are a common attack. You can disable them with --ignore-scripts. pnpm 10 blocks dependency build scripts unless allowlisted.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which practices reduce npm supply-chain risk?
options: Installing with npm ci from a committed lockfile
Using * ranges to always get the latest fixes
Running npm audit or Dependabot/Renovate in CI
Disabling install scripts where not needed
Publishing your packages with long-lived tokens stored in many CI jobs
questions.explanation: Locked installs, automated advisories and disabled install scripts all reduce exposure. Wildcard ranges pull in compromised versions automatically, and long-lived tokens are exactly what attackers steal; trusted publishing via OIDC is safer.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the range ___1.4.2 allows 1.4.x patch updates but not 1.5.0.
questions.explanation: The tilde range ~1.4.2 means >=1.4.2 <1.5.0. The caret would allow up to <2.0.0.

questions.prompt: Explain what a lockfile is and why npm ci exists.
questions.answer:
- package.json holds ranges; resolving them depends on what is published at install time, so installs drift.
- The lockfile captures the fully resolved tree: exact versions, where each was fetched from, and an integrity hash, so every install gets byte-identical packages.
- npm ci is the install command for automation: it wipes node_modules, installs strictly from the lockfile, never modifies it, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree. That gives reproducible builds and catches developers forgetting to commit lockfile changes.
- Dependency updates then become explicit, reviewable PRs (often by Renovate or Dependabot) rather than surprises in production.

questions.prompt: How do you protect a Node.js project from malicious or compromised npm packages?
questions.answer:
- Commit lockfiles, install with npm ci, and update via reviewed bot PRs with a minimum release age so freshly published (possibly malicious) versions are not adopted instantly.
- Limit install scripts (--ignore-scripts, pnpm's allowlist).
- Run npm audit / Socket / Snyk in CI and fail on critical issues; check new dependencies for maintenance, downloads and typosquats before adding.
- Keep the dependency count small; avoid trivial packages.
- For your own packages: enable 2FA, use trusted publishing with provenance instead of long-lived tokens.
- At runtime, apply least privilege: minimal secrets in the environment, containers without root, and consider Node's permission model for scripts.

questions.prompt: What are peerDependencies and when have you seen them cause problems?
questions.answer:
A peerDependency says "I work inside a host that provides X" (plugins for eslint, React component libraries, Express middleware sometimes). The consumer is expected to have exactly one compatible version.
Problems: since npm 7 peers are auto-installed, and conflicting peer ranges cause ERESOLVE errors; people then reach for --legacy-peer-deps, which hides real incompatibilities. Misdeclaring a peer as a regular dependency leads to two copies (the classic "invalid hook call" from two Reacts, or instanceof failing across copies).
The right fix is to align versions or upgrade the plugin, not to blanket-disable peer checks.

chapters.title: The event loop: phases, nextTick, microtasks and setImmediate
chapters.summary: Predict exactly when callbacks run by understanding the loop phases and the two queues drained between them.

lesson.heading: The six phases
lesson.body:
After the main script finishes, libuv runs the event loop. Each iteration (a "tick" of the loop) walks through phases, each with its own FIFO queue of callbacks:

- **timers**: callbacks from `setTimeout` and `setInterval` whose threshold has passed.
- **pending callbacks**: some system-level callbacks deferred from the previous iteration (e.g. certain TCP errors).
- **idle, prepare**: internal use.
- **poll**: retrieve new I/O events and run their callbacks (socket data, completed fs operations). If nothing else is scheduled, the loop blocks here waiting for I/O, up to the nearest timer.
- **check**: `setImmediate` callbacks.
- **close callbacks**: e.g. `socket.on("close")`.

The loop exits when there are no more referenced handles or requests: no active servers, timers, sockets or pending operations. `timer.unref()` lets a timer exist without keeping the process alive.

lesson.heading: Microtasks and the nextTick queue
lesson.body:
Two queues are not part of libuv's phases; Node drains them **after every individual callback** (and after the main script):

- The **process.nextTick queue** is drained first, completely.
- Then the **promise microtask queue** (`.then` callbacks, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`) is drained completely.
- If draining microtasks schedules more nextTicks, Node loops again until both queues are empty.

So in a CommonJS script: synchronous code first, then all nextTicks, then all promise callbacks, then the event loop phases (timers, poll, check...).

**ESM gotcha:** an ES module's top-level code is evaluated as part of a promise job. Promise callbacks queued there run before nextTick callbacks, so the same snippet can print `promise` before `nextTick` in a `.mjs` file. Never write code that relies on the relative order of nextTick and promises.

lesson.heading: setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate
lesson.body:
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` is really a 1 ms timer. `setImmediate(fn)` runs in the check phase of the current or next loop iteration.

- **From the main module**, their order is non-deterministic: it depends on whether 1 ms has elapsed by the time the loop enters the timers phase, which depends on process performance.
- **Inside an I/O callback** (poll phase), `setImmediate` always runs first, because the check phase comes right after poll, while timers wait for the next iteration.

Use `setImmediate` to yield to the event loop between chunks of work so pending I/O can be processed.

lesson.heading: When to use which
lesson.body:
- `process.nextTick(fn)`: run after the current operation, before any I/O. Used inside Node and libraries to emit events or errors asynchronously after the constructor returns, so callers can attach listeners. The Node docs recommend `queueMicrotask` or `setImmediate` for most userland code.
- `queueMicrotask(fn)` / promises: standard, cross-runtime microtask scheduling.
- `setImmediate(fn)`: yield to I/O, then continue. Good for splitting long CPU loops.
- `setTimeout(fn, ms)`: a minimum delay, never exact. Timers can fire late if the loop is busy.

**Starvation:** because nextTick and microtask queues are drained completely, a callback that keeps scheduling more nextTicks (or a promise chain that never yields) prevents the loop from ever reaching the poll phase. I/O stops being processed. `setImmediate` recursion does not starve I/O, since each iteration passes through poll.

lesson.heading: async/await on the loop
lesson.body:
`await` splits a function: everything after it is a microtask continuation. An `async` function runs synchronously until its first `await`.

`await` on an already-resolved value still defers the continuation to the microtask queue, so code after it runs after the current synchronous code finishes, but before timers and I/O.

Measuring loop health: `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` returns a histogram of loop delay, and `performance.eventLoopUtilization()` reports how busy the loop is. Rising p99 delay is the classic sign of blocking code.

keyPoints: Loop phases in order: timers, pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll, check, close callbacks.
After every callback Node drains the nextTick queue, then the promise microtask queue.
In CommonJS, nextTick callbacks run before promise callbacks; in ESM top-level code that order can flip.
setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate is non-deterministic in the main module, but setImmediate always wins inside an I/O callback.
Recursive nextTick or microtasks starve I/O; recursive setImmediate does not.
An async function runs synchronously until its first await.
Monitor loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay and eventLoopUtilization.

questions.prompt: In a CommonJS file, what is the output order?
questions.explanation: Synchronous logs A and E run first. Then the nextTick queue (D) is drained, then promise microtasks (C), then the event loop reaches the timers phase (B).

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The callback runs in the poll phase. The next phase is check, where setImmediate runs; timers only run on the next loop iteration. Inside I/O callbacks setImmediate is always first.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: f() runs synchronously until await, printing 1. Control returns to the caller, which prints 4. Then the microtask continuation prints 2, and the next await continuation prints 3.

questions.prompt: What is the output in a CommonJS file?
questions.explanation: Both promise callbacks are already in the microtask queue. Node drains the whole microtask queue before checking the nextTick queue again, so the nextTick scheduled inside p1 runs after p2.

questions.prompt: In which phase do setImmediate callbacks run?
questions.explanation: setImmediate callbacks are queued for the check phase, which runs right after the poll phase.

questions.prompt: A function recursively calls process.nextTick(itself) forever. What happens to incoming HTTP requests?
options: They are processed normally between ticks
They are never processed because the loop never reaches the poll phase
Node throws a RangeError for the nextTick queue
They are handled by the thread pool
questions.explanation: The nextTick queue is drained completely before the loop can move on. A self-replenishing queue starves I/O indefinitely. Using setImmediate instead would let each loop iteration pass through poll.

questions.prompt: setTimeout(fn, 100) guarantees fn runs exactly 100 ms later.
questions.explanation: The delay is a minimum. The callback runs in the first timers phase after 100 ms have passed, and can be much later if the main thread is busy.

questions.prompt: A Node process exits automatically when there are no pending timers, I/O operations, servers or other referenced handles.
questions.explanation: The event loop keeps running only while something is keeping it alive. unref() on a timer or server lets it not count toward this.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which run as promise microtasks (not nextTick and not a loop phase)?
options: Code after await in an async function
questions.explanation: then callbacks, await continuations and queueMicrotask all go to V8's microtask queue. setImmediate is the check phase, and nextTick has its own Node-managed queue that is drained before microtasks.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: inside an fs callback, use ___ to schedule work that is guaranteed to run before any setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled in the same callback.
questions.explanation: From the poll phase the loop proceeds to check (setImmediate) before wrapping around to timers.

questions.prompt: Walk me through the Node.js event loop phases and where process.nextTick and promises fit.
questions.answer:
- After the main module runs, libuv iterates: timers (expired setTimeout/setInterval), pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll (wait for and run I/O callbacks; blocks here if idle), check (setImmediate), close callbacks.
- process.nextTick and promise microtasks are not phases. After each callback, Node drains the nextTick queue completely, then the microtask queue completely, repeating until both are empty.
- Consequences: nextTick and promise callbacks run before any I/O or timers; setImmediate inside an I/O callback runs before timers; recursive nextTick/microtasks can starve I/O.
- In practice I use promises/async-await, setImmediate to yield in long loops, and avoid depending on micro-ordering between nextTick and promises (it differs between CJS and ESM).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between process.nextTick, setImmediate and setTimeout(fn, 0)?
questions.answer:
- process.nextTick: runs right after the current callback finishes, before promises and before the loop continues. Highest priority; can starve I/O if abused. Used by libraries to defer event emission until after the caller attaches listeners.
- setImmediate: runs in the check phase, after the current poll phase. Good for yielding to I/O. The naming is confusing: nextTick is more immediate than setImmediate.
- setTimeout(fn, 0): a 1 ms timer in the timers phase of a later iteration. Relative to setImmediate it is non-deterministic from the main module, but always after setImmediate when scheduled from an I/O callback.

questions.prompt: Your API's p99 latency spikes every few minutes while CPU stays moderate. How would you check whether the event loop is being blocked?
questions.answer:
- Measure event loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() (export p50/p99/max as metrics) and eventLoopUtilization(); spikes correlating with latency confirm blocking.
- Look for the cause: a CPU profile during a spike (node --cpu-prof, clinic flame, 0x, or the inspector) shows the hot synchronous function, often JSON.parse/stringify on large payloads, sync fs/crypto calls, a regex with catastrophic backtracking, a large sort, or a periodic job running in-process.
- Also check GC: --trace-gc or the GC entries in the profile; long major GCs from a growing heap look like blocking too.
- Fixes: stream or paginate large payloads, move CPU work to worker_threads or a job queue, chunk loops with setImmediate, replace sync APIs, fix the regex, cap request body sizes.

questions.prompt: Why might the same snippet print nextTick before promise in a .cjs file but the reverse in a .mjs file?
questions.answer:
In CommonJS the main script runs as a plain synchronous call; when it finishes Node drains the nextTick queue first, then microtasks.
An ES module's evaluation happens inside the module loader's promise machinery, so the top-level code is effectively already running in a microtask context. Promise callbacks queued there are drained as part of that same microtask checkpoint, before Node gets a chance to process the nextTick queue.
The lesson is that relative ordering of nextTick and promises is an implementation detail; code must not depend on it. If order matters, chain explicitly.

chapters.title: fs, path, Buffers and Streams
chapters.summary: Work with files and binary data efficiently, and use streams with backpressure to process data larger than memory.

lesson.heading: fs: three API styles
lesson.body:
`node:fs` offers the same operations in three styles:

- **Promise API** (`node:fs/promises`): `await readFile(path, "utf8")`. Default choice in application code.
- **Callback API** (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`): older style, still used in hot paths and older libraries.
- **Sync API** (`fs.readFileSync`): blocks the main thread. Fine for startup and CLI scripts, not in request handlers.

Useful modern helpers: `fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })`, `fs.rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })`, `fs.cp` for recursive copy, `fs.glob` (Node 22+) and `fs.watch`. Prefer handling errors over checking first: `access()` then `open()` is a race condition (TOCTOU). Just open and handle `ENOENT`.

lesson.heading: path and URL
lesson.body:
Never build paths by string concatenation. `path` handles separators (`/` vs `\` on Windows) and normalisation:

- `path.join("a", "../b", "c.txt")` -> `b/c.txt` (joins and normalises).
- `path.resolve("src", "app.js")` -> absolute path, resolved against `process.cwd()` unless an absolute segment appears.
- `path.basename`, `path.dirname`, `path.extname`, `path.parse`.
- `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` and `pathToFileURL(p)` convert between file URLs and paths.

Security: when joining user input into a path, resolve it and verify it stays inside the intended root, otherwise `../../etc/passwd` escapes (path traversal).

lesson.heading: Buffers: binary data
lesson.body:
A `Buffer` is a fixed-length sequence of bytes, a subclass of `Uint8Array`. Files, sockets and crypto produce Buffers unless you ask for a string encoding.

- Create: `Buffer.from("hello", "utf8")`, `Buffer.alloc(16)` (zero-filled), `Buffer.allocUnsafe(16)` (faster, may contain old memory: overwrite it fully before use).
- Convert: `buf.toString("base64")`, `"hex"`, `"utf8"`, `"base64url"`.
- Length is in **bytes**, not characters: `Buffer.byteLength("é")` is 2. Emojis are 4 bytes.
- `buf.subarray()` returns a view sharing memory, not a copy. Mutating it mutates the original.
- Compare secrets with `crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b)`, not `===`.

Splitting UTF-8 data at arbitrary chunk boundaries can cut a multi-byte character in half. Use `setEncoding("utf8")` on streams or `StringDecoder` instead of calling `toString()` on each chunk.

lesson.heading: Streams and backpressure
lesson.body:
Streams process data piece by piece, so memory stays flat no matter how big the input is. Four types: **Readable** (file read, HTTP request body), **Writable** (file write, HTTP response), **Duplex** (TCP socket), **Transform** (gzip, encryption, parsing).

**Backpressure**: when the consumer is slower than the producer, `writable.write()` returns `false` once its internal buffer passes `highWaterMark` (default 64 KiB for byte streams since Node 22, 16 objects in object mode). The producer should pause until the `drain` event. Ignoring this makes memory grow unbounded.

Use `pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises`. It wires streams together, handles backpressure, propagates errors from any stage and destroys every stream on failure. Plain `.pipe()` does **not** forward errors or clean up, which leaks file descriptors.

Readable streams are async iterables, so `for await (const chunk of stream)` consumes them with backpressure built in.

lesson.heading: Streaming HTTP responses
lesson.body:
An HTTP response is a Writable stream, so you can pipe a file or a database cursor straight into it. This keeps memory constant for large downloads and gets the first byte to the client quickly.

Web Streams (`ReadableStream`, `WritableStream`) are also implemented in Node, used by `fetch`. Convert with `Readable.fromWeb()` and `Readable.toWeb()`.

keyPoints: Use node:fs/promises in app code; sync fs APIs only at startup or in scripts.
Handle ENOENT instead of checking existence first, to avoid race conditions.
Build paths with path.join/resolve and guard against traversal when user input is involved.
Buffer length counts bytes; UTF-8 characters can be 1 to 4 bytes.
write() returning false means stop and wait for drain: that is backpressure.
Prefer stream/promises pipeline over .pipe(): it propagates errors and destroys all streams.
Readable streams are async iterables (for await...of).

questions.prompt: What does Buffer.from("é").length return?
questions.explanation: Buffer length is measured in bytes. The character e with acute accent (U+00E9) is encoded as 2 bytes in UTF-8, so the buffer length is 2 even though the string length is 1.

questions.prompt: Why is stream.pipeline() preferred over readable.pipe(writable)?
options: pipeline() forwards errors from every stage and destroys all streams on failure
questions.explanation: pipe() handles backpressure but does not propagate errors or clean up the other streams, leaking file descriptors and leaving requests hanging. pipeline() does both and gives you a single promise or callback.

questions.prompt: writable.write(chunk) returned false. What should a well-behaved producer do?
options: Stop writing until the writable emits drain
Nothing, false only means the chunk was small
questions.explanation: false means the internal buffer is above highWaterMark. The chunk was accepted, but continuing to write grows memory. Wait for drain, then resume. pipeline and for-await handle this automatically.

questions.prompt: What does path.join("/app", "uploads", "../config", "db.json") return on POSIX?
questions.explanation: path.join concatenates segments and normalises them, resolving the .. against the preceding segment. uploads/.. cancels out, leaving /app/config/db.json. This normalisation is also why user input must be checked after resolving.

questions.prompt: Which code is the safest way to compare an HMAC signature from a request to the expected one?
options: crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sig), Buffer.from(expected)) after checking lengths match
questions.explanation: String comparison stops at the first differing byte, leaking timing information an attacker can use to guess the signature byte by byte. timingSafeEqual takes constant time but throws if lengths differ, so check length first.

questions.prompt: You need to serve a 4 GB file over HTTP. Which approach keeps memory usage low?
questions.explanation: Streaming reads small chunks (64 KiB by default) and writes them as the socket accepts them, so memory stays flat. Reading the whole file would need 4 GB of memory and exceeds the maximum string size anyway.

questions.prompt: Checking fs.access() before fs.open() is the recommended way to avoid errors when a file might not exist.
questions.explanation: Between the check and the open, another process can create or delete the file (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The recommended approach is to open directly and handle ENOENT or EEXIST.

questions.prompt: buf.subarray(0, 4) returns a new Buffer that shares memory with buf.
questions.explanation: subarray (and the deprecated slice on Buffer) create a view over the same memory. Changing a byte in the view changes the original. Use Buffer.from(view) or copy() for an independent copy.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are Duplex or Transform streams?
questions.explanation: A TCP socket is Duplex (independent read and write sides). gzip and cipher streams are Transforms (output derived from input). A file read stream is Readable only, and ServerResponse is Writable.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: for await (const chunk of ___) works because Readable streams implement the async iterator protocol.
questions.explanation: Readable streams implement Symbol.asyncIterator, so for await...of reads chunks one at a time and naturally applies backpressure: the next chunk is only pulled after the loop body finishes.

questions.prompt: What is backpressure in Node.js streams and what happens if you ignore it?
questions.answer:
- Backpressure is the mechanism that slows a fast producer down to the speed of a slow consumer.
- Writable streams buffer incoming chunks; once the buffer exceeds highWaterMark, write() returns false. The producer should pause and resume on the drain event. Readable streams similarly stop reading from the source when their buffer is full and nobody is consuming.
- Ignoring it (calling write() in a loop regardless of the return value) means data piles up in memory: a fast disk read piped into a slow network client can grow the heap until the process crashes or GC thrashes.
- pipeline(), pipe() and for await...of handle this automatically, which is why they are preferred over manual data event handlers.

questions.prompt: How would you process a 20 GB CSV file in Node.js and insert rows into a database?
questions.answer:
- Stream it: createReadStream -> a CSV parser transform (e.g. csv-parse) in object mode -> a Writable or async iterator that batches rows (e.g. 1,000 at a time) and inserts each batch.
- Use for await...of or pipeline so the database speed controls the read speed (backpressure), keeping memory flat.
- Insert in batches or use the database's bulk path (COPY in Postgres via pg-copy-streams) inside transactions, with an idempotent strategy (upsert or a staging table) so the job can resume after failure; track progress by line or byte offset.
- Handle bad rows by logging them to an error file rather than failing the whole job, and run it as a background job, not inside an HTTP request.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between Buffer.alloc and Buffer.allocUnsafe.
questions.answer:
Buffer.alloc(size) allocates and zero-fills memory, so it is safe but slightly slower. Buffer.allocUnsafe(size) skips zero-filling and may draw from a shared pre-allocated pool, so it can contain old data from previous allocations (possibly secrets like tokens).
allocUnsafe is fine only when you immediately overwrite every byte (e.g. you are about to copy data into it). Otherwise returning or logging it can leak memory contents. Buffer.from and Buffer.concat already handle this correctly.

chapters.title: EventEmitter, error handling and graceful shutdown
chapters.summary: Use events correctly, handle sync and async errors without crashing or hiding bugs, and shut down cleanly.

lesson.heading: EventEmitter basics
lesson.body:
`EventEmitter` from `node:events` is the publish/subscribe primitive behind streams, servers, sockets and child processes. You register listeners with `on` (or `once`) and trigger them with `emit`.

Important behaviour:

- `emit` calls listeners **synchronously**, in registration order, and returns `true` if any listener existed.
- The `"error"` event is special: emitting it with no listener **throws** the error, which usually crashes the process.
- More than 10 listeners for one event logs a `MaxListenersExceededWarning`. It often signals a leak (adding a listener per request without removing it).
- `events.once(emitter, "name")` returns a promise, and `events.on(emitter, "name")` returns an async iterator.

lesson.heading: Operational vs programmer errors
lesson.body:
Two different categories need different handling:

- **Operational errors** are expected failures in a correct program: a network timeout, `ENOENT`, invalid user input, a DB unique constraint. Handle them: retry, return a 4xx/5xx, fall back.
- **Programmer errors** are bugs: reading a property of `undefined`, wrong argument types, a forgotten `await`. You cannot recover meaningfully; fix the code. If one escapes to the top level, the process state may be corrupt.

Throw `Error` objects (never strings) so you get stack traces, and add context with `cause`: `throw new Error("Failed to load user", { cause: err })`. Custom error classes with a `code` or `status` make handling explicit.

lesson.heading: Async error patterns and their traps
lesson.body:
- **Callbacks**: error-first convention `(err, result)`. A `throw` inside an async callback cannot be caught by a surrounding `try/catch`, because the try block finished long ago.
- **Promises**: errors flow to the nearest `.catch()`. With `async/await`, `try/catch` works only if you actually `await` the promise.
- **Forgotten await**: `try { doAsync(); } catch {}` catches nothing. The rejection becomes unhandled.
- **return vs return await**: inside a try block, `return promise` exits the try before the promise settles, so its rejection skips your catch. Use `return await` there.

`Promise.all` rejects on the first failure (other promises keep running). Use `Promise.allSettled` when you need every result.

lesson.heading: Process-level handlers
lesson.body:
Since Node 15, an **unhandled promise rejection** crashes the process by default (`--unhandled-rejections=throw`), exactly like an uncaught exception. That is the right default: it surfaces bugs instead of silently hiding them.

`process.on("uncaughtException")` and `process.on("unhandledRejection")` are for **last-resort logging**, then exit. Do not use them to keep serving traffic, because the process may hold half-finished state (open transactions, locks). Let your supervisor (Kubernetes, systemd, PM2) restart it.

lesson.heading: Cancellation and graceful shutdown
lesson.body:
`AbortController` is the standard cancellation primitive. Pass `signal` to `fetch`, `fs` methods, `events.once`, timers from `node:timers/promises` and many libraries. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` creates a signal that aborts automatically, and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` combines signals.

Graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM` (what Kubernetes and Docker send before `SIGKILL`):

- Stop accepting new connections: `server.close()`. Mark readiness probes as failing.
- Let in-flight requests finish, with a hard timeout. `server.closeIdleConnections()` releases idle keep-alive sockets.
- Close resources: DB pools, Redis, message consumers. Flush logs.
- Exit with code 0, or force-exit after the timeout.

In containers, run node as PID 1 carefully: use `exec node server.js` (not `npm start`, which may not forward signals) or an init like `tini`.

keyPoints: emit() runs listeners synchronously, in registration order.
An "error" event with no listener throws and usually crashes the process.
MaxListenersExceededWarning usually means a listener leak.
Handle operational errors; fix programmer errors and let the process restart if one escapes.
try/catch only catches async errors you await; use return await inside try.
Unhandled rejections crash the process by default since Node 15.
Use AbortController/AbortSignal.timeout for cancellation and handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: emit calls all listeners synchronously before returning. So the listener prints A between B and C.

questions.prompt: What happens when this runs?
options: The error is thrown from emit() and, uncaught, crashes the process
The error is passed to process.on("warning")
questions.explanation: If an EventEmitter emits "error" and there is no listener for it, Node throws the error from emit(). Always attach an error listener to emitters that can fail (streams, sockets, clients).

questions.prompt: Why does the catch block never run when fetchUser rejects?
options: return without await leaves the try block before the promise settles
catch blocks do not work in async functions
The error is a programmer error
questions.explanation: return fetchUser() hands the pending promise back to the caller immediately, so the try block is already finished when it rejects. return await keeps the function suspended inside try until settlement.

questions.prompt: By default in Node 24, what happens on an unhandled promise rejection?
options: A warning is printed and execution continues
The process exits with an error, like an uncaught exception
questions.explanation: Since Node 15 the default mode is throw: an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, which terminates the process unless an uncaughtException handler intervenes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about process.on("uncaughtException") is the recommended practice?
options: Use it to keep the server running after any error
Use it to log synchronously and then exit, letting a supervisor restart the process
It replaces the need for try/catch
questions.explanation: After an uncaught exception the application state is unknown. The handler should log the error and exit. Restart and redundancy come from the orchestrator (Kubernetes, systemd, PM2).

questions.prompt: Which call aborts a fetch that takes longer than 5 seconds?
questions.explanation: fetch has no timeout option. AbortSignal.timeout creates a signal that aborts with a TimeoutError DOMException after the delay.

questions.prompt: A try/catch around a call that schedules a callback with setTimeout will catch errors thrown inside that callback.
questions.explanation: The callback runs later on a fresh call stack, after the try block has completed. Errors thrown there are uncaught. Use promises with await, or handle errors inside the callback.

questions.prompt: Promise.all rejects as soon as one input promise rejects, but the other promises keep running.
questions.explanation: Promises are not cancellable; Promise.all only stops waiting. If the other work should stop, pass an AbortSignal to each operation. Use allSettled when you need every outcome.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are operational errors rather than programmer errors?
options: ECONNREFUSED when calling a downstream API
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
A user submits an invalid email
Calling a function with the wrong number of arguments due to a typo
Disk full (ENOSPC) while writing a file
questions.explanation: Network failures, invalid input and disk full are conditions a correct program must anticipate and handle. Reading properties of undefined and wrong call signatures are bugs to fix.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: throw new Error("Failed to save order", { ___: err }) preserves the original error.
questions.explanation: The cause option (ES2022) attaches the underlying error, and Node prints it in stack traces. It keeps context without losing the original error's stack.

questions.prompt: How do you handle errors in an async Node.js application end to end?
questions.answer:
- Distinguish operational errors (handle: retry with backoff, translate to HTTP status, fallback) from programmer errors (fix; let them crash).
- Use async/await with try/catch where you can actually do something; otherwise let errors propagate. Throw Error subclasses with codes, wrap with cause for context.
- In web frameworks, use a central error middleware that maps known errors to responses and logs unknown ones with request IDs, without leaking stack traces to clients.
- Attach error listeners to every EventEmitter/stream, and use pipeline for streams.
- At process level, log unhandledRejection/uncaughtException and exit; rely on the orchestrator to restart, and run multiple instances.
- Add timeouts (AbortSignal.timeout) to all outbound calls so errors surface instead of hanging.

questions.prompt: How would you implement graceful shutdown for a Node.js HTTP service running in Kubernetes?
questions.answer:
- Listen for SIGTERM (Kubernetes sends it, then SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30s).
- Flip readiness to failing so the Service stops routing new traffic; optionally wait a few seconds for endpoint propagation.
- Call server.close() to stop accepting connections, closeIdleConnections() for idle keep-alive sockets, and let in-flight requests complete.
- Stop queue consumers from pulling new jobs and let current jobs finish or requeue them.
- Close DB pools, Redis and broker connections, flush logs/metrics, then exit 0.
- Set a hard timeout shorter than the grace period that force-exits. Make sure node actually receives the signal: exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] or tini, not npm start.

questions.prompt: You see MaxListenersExceededWarning in production logs. What does it mean and what do you do?
questions.answer:
It means more than 10 (the default) listeners were added to one event on one emitter. Usually that is a leak: code calls emitter.on() per request or per retry on a long-lived object (a shared socket, DB client, process) and never removes the listener, so memory and work grow over time.
I would use the warning's stack trace (run with --trace-warnings) to find where listeners are added, then fix it: use once(), remove listeners on completion, use AbortSignal-based listeners, or restructure so one listener dispatches to many handlers.
Only raise setMaxListeners when a high, bounded listener count is genuinely by design.

chapters.title: Built-in test runner, configuration, security basics and modern Node
chapters.summary: Use what ships in Node 22 and 24: node:test, --env-file, TypeScript type stripping, --watch, the permission model, and secure coding defaults.

lesson.heading: The built-in test runner
lesson.body:
`node:test` is stable and covers most unit and integration testing without installing Jest or Vitest: `test`/`describe`/`it`, hooks (`before`, `beforeEach`, `after`, `afterEach`), subtests, mocking (`mock.fn`, `mock.method`, `mock.timers`), snapshot tests and reporters (spec, tap, junit, lcov).

Run `node --test` to auto-discover files like `*.test.js`, `test/**/*.js` or `*_test.mjs`. Add `--watch` for re-runs and `--experimental-test-coverage` (or `--test-coverage-*` options) for coverage. Pair it with `node:assert/strict`.

Jest and Vitest are still common in existing codebases (Vitest especially for Vite and TypeScript-heavy front ends), so know both worlds.

lesson.heading: Configuration and environment variables
lesson.body:
Follow the twelve-factor rule: config that varies per environment (URLs, credentials, feature flags) comes from environment variables, not from code.

- `node --env-file=.env app.js` loads a dotenv file natively (Node 20.6+). `--env-file-if-exists` does not fail when the file is missing. `process.loadEnvFile()` and `util.parseEnv()` do the same from code. The `dotenv` package is no longer required.
- Real environment variables take precedence over the file.
- **Validate config once at startup** and fail fast with a clear message. Parse types (numbers, booleans, URLs) instead of sprinkling `process.env.X` around the code.
- Never commit `.env` files with real secrets; commit a `.env.example`. In production, inject secrets from a secrets manager.

`NODE_ENV=production` matters: Express and many libraries enable caching and disable verbose errors based on it.

lesson.heading: TypeScript and dev workflow without extra tools
lesson.body:
**Type stripping**: Node 22.18+ and Node 23.6+ run `.ts` files directly by erasing type annotations (no type checking). Only erasable syntax works out of the box: enums, namespaces and parameter properties need `--experimental-transform-types`, or should be avoided. Use `import type` for type-only imports, include `.ts` extensions in relative imports, and keep running `tsc --noEmit` in CI for type checking.

- `node --watch app.js` restarts on file changes (replaces nodemon for most cases).
- `node --run test` runs a package.json script quickly.
- `node --inspect` opens the Chrome DevTools debugger.
- Single executable applications (SEA) bundle a script into a Node binary.

lesson.heading: Security basics for Node code
lesson.body:
- **Never pass user input to a shell.** `exec("convert " + filename)` is command injection. Use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array (no shell).
- **Avoid `eval`, `new Function`, and `vm` for untrusted code.** The `vm` module is not a security sandbox.
- **Prototype pollution**: merging untrusted JSON into objects can set `__proto__` and affect every object. Validate input with schemas, use `Object.create(null)` or `Map` for dictionaries, and use `--disable-proto=delete` if feasible.
- **ReDoS**: regexes with nested quantifiers like `(a+)+$` can take exponential time on crafted input and block the loop. Limit input length and test regexes.
- **Limit request sizes** and set timeouts (`server.requestTimeout`, `headersTimeout`).
- **Keep Node patched**: security releases land on all supported lines. Run as a non-root user in containers.

The **permission model** (`--permission`, stable since Node 23.5 and in Node 24) restricts file system, child process, worker and native addon access: `node --permission --allow-fs-read=./data app.js`. It is a defence-in-depth seatbelt for scripts and tools, not a sandbox for hostile code.

lesson.heading: What is new in Node 22 and 24
lesson.body:
Node 22 (LTS 2024): `require(esm)` unflagged (22.12), `--run`, stable `--watch`, global `WebSocket` client, `fs.glob`, `node:sqlite` (experimental), type stripping (22.18), 64 KiB default stream highWaterMark, Maglev compiler enabled.

Node 24 (LTS October 2025): V8 13.6 with `RegExp.escape`, `Float16Array`, `Error.isError` and explicit resource management (`using` and `await using` declarations that call `[Symbol.dispose]` automatically); global `URLPattern`; npm 11; undici 7 powering `fetch`; `AsyncLocalStorage` built on AsyncContextFrame by default; the permission model without the experimental flag; the test runner waits for subtests automatically.

keyPoints: node:test plus node:assert/strict cover unit tests, mocks, timers and snapshots without dependencies.
--env-file loads .env natively; validate and type config once at startup and fail fast.
Node 22.18+/23.6+ strip TypeScript types natively; type checking still needs tsc.
Use execFile/spawn with argument arrays, never exec with user input.
Watch for prototype pollution and ReDoS in code that handles untrusted input.
--permission restricts fs, child_process and workers; it is defence in depth, not a sandbox.
Node 24 brings using declarations, URLPattern, RegExp.escape and npm 11.

questions.prompt: Which command runs a Node app with variables loaded from .env without any npm package?
questions.explanation: --env-file has been built in since Node 20.6. -r dotenv/config needs the dotenv package. The other options do not exist or do something else.

questions.prompt: If PORT=8080 is set in the shell and .env contains PORT=3000, what does process.env.PORT equal with --env-file=.env?
questions.explanation: Variables already present in the environment take precedence over values from the env file, so deployment platforms can override file defaults.

questions.prompt: You run node app.ts on Node 24 and the file uses a TypeScript enum. What happens?
options: It runs fine, enums are erasable
It fails: enums need --experimental-transform-types because they generate runtime code
Node compiles it with tsc automatically
questions.explanation: Type stripping only removes syntax that has no runtime effect. Enums, namespaces with values and parameter properties emit JavaScript, so they require transformation. Node never type-checks.

questions.prompt: Which call is safe from shell command injection when filename comes from a user?
questions.explanation: execFile runs the binary directly without a shell, so metacharacters like ; or && in filename are passed as literal text. The others all go through a shell that interprets them.

questions.prompt: What does this print on Node 24?
questions.explanation: A using declaration calls [Symbol.dispose] when its block exits. The block ends after start is logged, so dispose runs before the code after the block.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of this function?
options: It is slow for large objects
Prototype pollution: a payload containing __proto__ can add properties to every object
questions.explanation: With JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}'), the recursive merge walks into Object.prototype and sets isAdmin on every object in the process. Skip __proto__, constructor and prototype keys, or validate with a schema.

questions.prompt: The node:vm module is a safe way to run untrusted user code.
questions.explanation: The Node docs state vm is not a security mechanism. Code can escape the context via prototype chains. Use a separate process with OS-level isolation, a container, or a purpose-built isolate for untrusted code.

questions.prompt: node --test can discover and run test files without any test framework installed.
questions.explanation: The built-in runner finds files matching default patterns (like **/*.test.js and files under test/) and executes them, reporting results with the spec reporter in a terminal.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which features are built into current Node LTS releases?
options: Full TypeScript type checking at runtime
questions.explanation: node:test, --env-file, --watch and the global WebSocket client are all built in. Node strips types but never type-checks; you still need tsc for that.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: node ___ --allow-fs-read=./config app.js enables the permission model and only allows reading ./config.
questions.explanation: --permission turns on the permission model; then access is denied by default and granted with flags like --allow-fs-read, --allow-fs-write, --allow-child-process and --allow-worker.

questions.prompt: How do you manage configuration and secrets in a Node.js service?
questions.answer:
- Environment-specific values come from environment variables (twelve-factor), with sensible non-secret defaults in code and a committed .env.example.
- Load and validate everything once at startup with a schema (Zod, envalid): parse numbers, booleans and URLs, and fail fast with a clear error if anything is missing.
- Export a typed config object; the rest of the code never touches process.env directly.
- Locally use --env-file; in production, inject secrets from a manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault, Doppler) via the platform, never bake them into images or commit them.
- Rotate secrets, scope them per service, and avoid logging config objects that contain secrets (redact in the logger).

questions.prompt: What are the most common security mistakes you see in Node.js code?
questions.answer:
- Command injection via exec with string concatenation; fix with execFile/spawn argument arrays.
- Injection into SQL/NoSQL queries built from strings; use parameterised queries and schema validation (e.g. reject objects where strings are expected to stop $ne operator injection in MongoDB).
- Prototype pollution from deep-merging untrusted input.
- ReDoS from vulnerable regexes on unbounded input, and missing body size limits, both of which can block the event loop.
- Path traversal when joining user input into file paths.
- Leaking stack traces or secrets in error responses and logs.
- Outdated dependencies and Node versions; no lockfile; running as root in containers.

questions.prompt: Would you use the built-in node:test runner or Jest/Vitest for a new backend service? Justify.
questions.answer:
For a new pure Node backend, node:test is a solid default: zero dependencies, fast startup, native ESM and TypeScript (via type stripping), mocking including timers, watch mode, coverage and JUnit reporters for CI.
Jest or Vitest still win when the team relies on their richer ecosystem: Vitest's fast watch mode, in-source tests, browser mode and Vite-based transforms; Jest's mature snapshot and module mocking (jest.mock style hoisted mocks), and existing large suites.
Module-level mocking is the main gap: node:test has mock.module behind a flag. Designing code with dependency injection makes that gap mostly irrelevant. In a monorepo with a Vite front end I'd likely standardise on Vitest for consistency.

chapters.title: Scaling Node: worker_threads, child_process and cluster
chapters.summary: Choose the right tool to use multiple cores: threads for CPU work, processes for isolation and external programs, cluster or replicas for throughput.

lesson.heading: Three ways to use more than one core
lesson.body:
A single Node process runs your JavaScript on one core. To use more:

- **worker_threads**: extra V8 isolates (each with its own event loop and heap) inside the same process. Cheap messaging, can share memory. For CPU-bound JavaScript.
- **child_process**: separate OS processes. For running other programs (ffmpeg, git, Python) or fully isolated Node scripts.
- **cluster**: forks N copies of your server that share one listening port. For throughput of an HTTP server on one machine.

In containerised deployments the usual approach is simpler: run **one Node process per container** and scale replicas horizontally with Kubernetes or your platform. Use worker threads for CPU hot spots inside a service.

lesson.heading: worker_threads
lesson.body:
Each worker has its own isolate, event loop and module graph. Communication is by message passing (`postMessage`), which uses the structured clone algorithm (copies data). To avoid copying:

- **Transfer** an `ArrayBuffer` (ownership moves, zero-copy; the sender can no longer use it).
- **Share** a `SharedArrayBuffer` and coordinate with `Atomics` (true shared memory).

Starting a worker costs tens of milliseconds and memory, so use a **pool** (Piscina is the standard library) rather than a worker per request. Workers do not help I/O-bound work: the main thread is already non-blocking for I/O.

lesson.heading: child_process
lesson.body:
- `spawn(cmd, args)`: streams stdin/stdout/stderr. Best for long-running or large-output commands.
- `execFile(file, args)`: buffers output, no shell. Good for short commands.
- `exec(command)`: runs through a shell and buffers output (`maxBuffer` default 1 MiB). Convenient but injection-prone with user input.
- `fork(modulePath)`: spawns a new Node process with an IPC channel (`process.send` / `on("message")`).

Child processes give full isolation: a crash or memory leak in the child does not take down the parent, and you can kill it on timeout. The cost is higher memory and slower startup than threads.

lesson.heading: cluster and load balancing
lesson.body:
`cluster` forks worker processes that share the server port. The primary process accepts connections and distributes them round-robin to workers (the default on all platforms except Windows). If a worker dies, the primary can fork a new one.

Caveats:

- Workers share **no memory**. In-memory sessions, caches or rate-limit counters become per-worker and inconsistent. Store shared state in Redis or a database.
- WebSocket and sticky-session protocols need sticky routing.
- PM2's cluster mode wraps the same mechanism.

In Kubernetes, prefer one process per pod and let the platform replicate. Clustering inside a pod complicates CPU limits, health checks and metrics.

lesson.heading: The libuv thread pool as a hidden bottleneck
lesson.body:
Async `fs`, `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt/randomBytes` (async variants) and `zlib` share the default **4-thread** pool. If you hash passwords with bcrypt (native) or scrypt under load, those calls can queue behind slow file reads, and vice versa. Symptoms: latency climbs while CPU is not saturated.

Mitigations: raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (set it in the environment, before startup), move heavy hashing into a dedicated worker pool, cache DNS or use `dns.resolve` (which uses c-ares, not the pool), and avoid sync variants on the main thread.

`AsyncLocalStorage` (from `node:async_hooks`) is the standard way to carry request context (request ID, user, trace) across async boundaries, including into worker callbacks, without passing it through every function.

keyPoints: worker_threads: same process, separate isolates; for CPU-bound JavaScript; use a pool.
